title: The new database pod is stuck Pending (PVC never binds)
intro: A developer deployed a new 'orders-db' StatefulSet in the 'orders' namespace. Its first pod, orders-db-0, has been Pending for 15 minutes. The cluster has plenty of CPU and memory free.

steps.prompt: Describe the pod orders-db-0 in the orders namespace and read its Events.
steps.fake_output:
Events:
  Warning  FailedScheduling  default-scheduler  0/3 nodes are available: pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims. preemption: 0/3 nodes are available: 3 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling.
steps.hint: Pending pods almost always explain themselves in the Events at the bottom of describe.

steps.prompt: It isn't a resources problem: the pod is waiting for its volume claim to bind. List the PVCs in the orders namespace.
steps.fake_output:
NAME               STATUS    VOLUME   CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS   AGE
data-orders-db-0   Pending                                      fast-ssd       15m
steps.hint: StatefulSets create one PVC per pod from volumeClaimTemplates, named <template>-<pod>.

steps.prompt: Describe the PVC data-orders-db-0 to see why it isn't binding.
steps.fake_output:
Events:
  Warning  ProvisioningFailed  persistentvolume-controller  storageclass.storage.k8s.io "fast-ssd" not found
steps.hint: describe works on PVCs too, and their Events come from the provisioner.

steps.prompt: The claim asks for a StorageClass called 'fast-ssd' that doesn't exist. List the StorageClasses this cluster actually has.
steps.fake_output:
NAME                 PROVISIONER             RECLAIMPOLICY   VOLUMEBINDINGMODE      AGE
standard (default)   ebs.csi.aws.com         Delete          WaitForFirstConsumer   300d
gp3-ssd              ebs.csi.aws.com         Delete          WaitForFirstConsumer   300d
steps.hint: The short name is sc. Note which class is marked (default).

steps.prompt: The SSD class here is called gp3-ssd; 'fast-ssd' was copied from another cluster's manifest. PVC specs can't be edited after creation, and a StatefulSet doesn't recreate its PVCs when you change its template. So fix storageClassName in the manifest, then delete the stuck claim data-orders-db-0 so the StatefulSet recreates it.
steps.hint: kubectl delete pvc <name> -n <namespace>. It's safe here because it never bound, so there is no data.

steps.prompt: After re-applying the corrected StatefulSet and deleting pod orders-db-0 so it's recreated, watch the new claim bind.
steps.fake_output:
NAME               STATUS    VOLUME                                     CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS   AGE
data-orders-db-0   Pending                                                                        gp3-ssd        2s
data-orders-db-0   Bound     pvc-7e1c2b9a-4d6f-4a8e-9f0b-1c2d3e4f5a6b   20Gi       RWO            gp3-ssd        6s
steps.hint: -w (--watch) streams changes until you press Ctrl+C.

resolution: The pod never had a scheduling problem, it had a storage one: 'unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims' means the scheduler is waiting on a claim, and the claim's own Events named a StorageClass that doesn't exist in this cluster. The trap is how sticky PVCs are. volumeClaimTemplates only create claims, never update them, and a PVC's storageClassName is immutable, so fixing the StatefulSet YAML alone changes nothing until the old claim is deleted. That was safe here because it never bound; on a claim that has bound, deleting it can destroy data if the reclaim policy is Delete. Prevention: don't hardcode StorageClass names across clusters (omit it to get the default, or template it per environment), and alert on PVCs Pending for more than a few minutes. Also note the WaitForFirstConsumer binding mode: with it, a PVC showing Pending before any pod uses it is normal, not a failure.
